title: Commentary on the Water Classic
subtitle: Li Daoyuan · Rivers as the Thread · A Millennial Index to China's Ancient Sites
description: Li Daoyuan (466–527), courtesy name Shanchang, was a native of Zhuozhou, Fanyang, and a geographer of the Northern Wei. Annotating the Eastern Han Water Classic by Sang Qin, he produced a work of forty volumes, documenting mountains, cities, ancient sites, and legends along 1,252 rivers across the country, citing over four hundred sources. It is the greatest geographical work of ancient China. This route follows the waterways of the Commentary on the Water Classic, visiting the nationally protected heritage sites that Li Daoyuan preserved in words.

route.title: Commentary on the Water Classic: Tracing 1,252 Rivers, Seeking China's Millennial Heritage
route.intro:
The greatest of all things under heaven is water—it floats the sky and bears the earth, reaches every height and depth, and moistens all things without exception.
Li Daoyuan (466–527), a Northern Wei geographer, was born into a family of officials. He lived through the chaotic era of the Northern and Southern Dynasties, when the Northern Wei held the north, the Southern Dynasties the south, and the land of Huaxia was split in two. But Li Daoyuan's pen recognized no boundaries—taking the Eastern Han Water Classic as his base, he devoted half a lifetime to expanding a slim work covering only 137 rivers into a monumental opus documenting 1,252 waterways. The Commentary on the Water Classic is not only a geography book but also a cultural map with waterways as its organizing thread. On the banks of every river, the ancient cities, ancient temples, ancient steles, and ancient battlefields could not escape his meticulous strokes. He crossed mountains and forded streams, went to sites in person, traveled up and down the great rivers in a time of war, and left behind the most complete geographical memory of Huaxia in words. Let us follow in Li Daoyuan's footsteps—from the roars of the Yellow River to the vastness of the Yangtze, from the vicissitudes of the Wei River to the cool clarity of the Luo River—taking water as our road and words as our boat, to seek the undying light of ancient sites.

stops.title: Stop One: The Yellow River's Waters Descend from Heaven
stops.content: Li Daoyuan's Yellow River was a great river brimming with life and destructive power. In the Commentary on the Water Classic, he devoted five entire volumes to the Yellow River, from its source in the Kunlun Mountains to its eastward entry into the sea, recording countless ferries, ancient capitals, and battlefields along its banks. The most magnificent section of the Yellow River is at Longmen (Dragon Gate)—on both banks, cliff faces rise like sheer knife-cuts, and the river roars through a narrow stone gateway. This is the legendary place where Yu the Great "chiseled the Dragon Gate" to control the floods. On the cliffs of these Dragon Gate banks, the Longmen Grottoes, carved during the reign of Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei, face the mountains and overlook the Yi River. Over two thousand niches and more than one hundred thousand Buddha images gaze serenely northward as the Yi River flows past. When Li Daoyuan passed through, perhaps the first grottoes had just been carved—he may have witnessed the craftsmen swinging their hammers on the precipices. A thousand years later, the smile of the Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple is still reflected in the Yi River, as if echoing Li Daoyuan's exclamation in the Commentary on the Water Classic: "Water is not a stone chisel, yet it can penetrate stone." Further downstream along the Yellow River, the Yongle Palace in Ruicheng, Shanxi—though built in the Yuan dynasty, long after Li Daoyuan's time—houses the "Procession of Celestial Worthies" mural, with nearly three hundred Daoist immortals parading to pay homage to the Primordial Celestial Worthy. Its sweeping, grand design shares the same spirit as the Yellow River's surging power. Yongle Palace originally stood in Yongle Town by the Yellow River, and was relocated entirely in 1959 due to the Sanmenxia Reservoir construction. This itself echoes the cities that moved with shifting waterways as Li Daoyuan described—when water changes course, people follow, but culture never ceases to flow. Li Daoyuan's depiction of the Yellow River in the Commentary on the Water Classic goes beyond geography to a profound compassion. He wrote that below Mengjin, the river "races like an arrow, drifting logs like flying arrows," and every flood season "the riverbanks burst, sweeping away homes"—this is the Yellow River as a "river of disasters." But he also enthusiastically recorded the wisdom of the people living along the Yellow River in coexisting with floods: "the people mostly build elevated platforms to avoid the water," and some villages "take boats as their homes and fishing as their livelihood." On the riverbank, Li Daoyuan also saw Han dynasty "stone figures"—ancient hydrological measuring devices: "a stone man stands in the water, with water-level marks carved on his body"—the world's earliest known water-level observation instruments. The most moving stretch of the Yellow River is at Hukou—"a hundred-fathom hanging waterfall, foam and spray surging and boiling." Li Daoyuan tied a rope around his waist and had the boatman lower him to the edge of the cliff to view the waterfall. "Flying spray soaked my clothes, cold penetrated to the bone." His willingness to risk danger in the pursuit of investigation was a kind of lonely bravery in the war-torn Northern and Southern Dynasties—a frail geographer who measured half the Yellow River on foot.

stops.title: Stop Two: The Huai River—A Corridor of Ancient Sites on the North-South Divide
stops.content: The Huai River is the dividing line between north and south China. The Commentary on the Water Classic devotes an independent volume to the "Huai River." Li Daoyuan paid particular attention to the ancient inscriptions and city sites on both banks of the Huai—because it lay on the front line of the north-south divide, many sites had been destroyed by war, and he was using his words to give them a last rescue. The Commentary reads: "The Huai River flows eastward, passing north of the old city of Shouchun." Shouchun is present-day Shou County, Anhui—the capital to which the Chu state moved at the end of the Warring States period, called Ying. This ancient city, guarding the middle reaches of the Huai River, had been a military flashpoint since antiquity. The Eastern Jin's famous Battle of the Fei River, a classic victory of the few over the many, took place on the Fei River outside Shouchun's walls—eight thousand Northern Mansion troops routing the million-strong Former Qin army. "Wind and crane, grass and trees—all seemed like enemy soldiers"—the story still echoes through military history. But Shouchun's vitality extends far beyond warfare. Still standing on the banks of the Huai River today is the Shou County Ancient City Wall, first built in the Song dynasty and repeatedly renovated through the Ming and Qing. The wall is over seven kilometers in circumference and about eight meters tall, with four towering gates. Its most remarkable feature is its flood control system—hidden drainage gates beneath the stone foundation. Whenever the Huai River floods, the townsfolk close the city gates and open the sluice gates, turning the entire city into a giant "flood-control ark." The wisdom of "building elevated platforms to avoid water," which Li Daoyuan observed along the Huai River, finds its most perfect continuation in the Shou County city wall. Today, strolling along the wall, looking out over the Huai River like a silken ribbon and the boundless fertile plains—the spirit of Li Daoyuan's rigorous field investigations seems to flow through every brick and tile. The Huai River stories recorded in the Commentary on the Water Classic stand as firm as this wall against the storms of time.

stops.title: Stop Three: The Yangtze River—The Great River Eastward Flows, Washing Away Ages of Heroes
stops.content: The Yangtze River occupies the most important position in the Commentary on the Water Classic. From the source of the Min River to its estuary, Li Daoyuan entitled it the "Jiang River" and wrote three lengthy volumes. Although he had not traveled the entire Yangtze in person, through collecting documents and interviewing travelers, he rendered a ten-thousand-mile river as if before his eyes. He began with the Three Gorges, exclaiming: "For seven hundred miles through the Three Gorges, mountains join on both banks without a single break"—this passage was later selected for school textbooks. Wu Gorge and Xiling Gorge, in his telling, are nothing less than "the peril of the Three Gorges." After the gorges, the Yangtze enters the land of Jing-Chu. Li Daoyuan recorded in particular the place where the Han River joins the Yangtze—"the rivers pay homage to the sovereign, a scene of majestic grandeur." On Mount Wudang, at this very confluence, Ming emperor Chengzu ordered the construction of the seventy-kilometer-long Wudang Mountains Architecture Complex, with its gilded bronze Golden Hall and magnificent Purple Cloud Palace. If Li Daoyuan had known of it from the underworld, he would surely have added a note to his river commentary: "On the mountain stands a palace complex of consummate craftsmanship." Further down the Yangtze, at the mouth of Lake Dongting, Li Daoyuan wrote: "Lake Dongting, five hundred li in circumference, where the sun and moon seem to rise and set within it"—a vast, boundless expanse. The Yueyang Tower on the lake's shore, first built in the late Eastern Han period, is as old as the Commentary on the Water Classic itself. Li Daoyuan, when writing his commentary, may have seen its predecessor—Lu Su's reviewing tower. A thousand years later, Fan Zhongyan's lines "worry before the world's worries" transformed this wooden tower into the spiritual landmark of all Chinese scholars. From Li Daoyuan's Water Classic to Fan Zhongyan's Record of Yueyang Tower, Chinese scholars have always been building monuments to mountains and rivers with their words. Li Daoyuan's portrayal of the Yangtze's Three Gorges is an adventure narrative staked on life itself. In his commentary, he wrote: "For seven hundred miles through the Three Gorges, mountains join on both banks without a single break. Layered cliffs and stacked peaks block out the sky and hide the sun"—arguably the classic description of a gorge in Chinese literature, later adapted directly into school textbooks. He recorded in detail the positions and names of the dangerous rapids: "Green Rapids, Xie Rapids, Kongling Rapids are the most dangerous of the Three Gorges." He even provided safe passage windows—"when the water rises, large boats can pass; when the water falls, only small boats can navigate"—such practical navigation guides show that the Commentary on the Water Classic also served as a manual of waterways and transport. Most breathtaking is Li Daoyuan's description of the "Goddess Peak." He quoted the local boatmen's legend: "The goddess of Mount Wu brings rain at dusk and clouds at dawn"—Song Yu's famous lines from his "Rhapsody on Gaotang" were skillfully woven into a geographical work. "On every clear early morning or frosty dawn, the woods are cold and the streams silent; often a high gibbon utters a long, mournful cry, its desolate note echoing through the empty valley, lingering long before fading away"—as you read these sentences, you can almost hear the gibbons calling. Li Daoyuan was not a poet, but his geographical notes are more moving than many poems.

stops.title: Stop Four: The Wei River—A Cultural Corridor Through the Eight-Hundred-Li Qinchuan Plain
stops.content: The Wei River is the Yellow River's largest tributary and the mother river of the Guanzhong Plain. The Commentary on the Water Classic devotes three volumes to the "Wei River," meticulously recording this river that nourished the Zhou, Qin, Han, and Tang dynasties. Li Daoyuan traveled westward along the Wei—entering the pass at Tong Pass, passing through Huayin and Lintong, and arriving at the foot of Chang'an City. Standing on the banks of the Wei, he beheld the grandeur of "eight hundred li of Qinchuan Plain, with the Wei River running through it." In Chang'an, the structures that most impressed Li Daoyuan were the Buddhist temples. Though the Great Wild Goose Pagoda had not yet been built in his time—that was Master Xuanzang's creation over a century after Li Daoyuan's death—he meticulously recorded the origins of several dozen Buddhist temples in and around Chang'an. The Great Wild Goose Pagoda, standing south of present-day Xi'an, is the living continuation of the temple records in the Commentary on the Water Classic. Xuanzang built this seven-story square pagoda to house the Sanskrit sutras he brought back from his westward journey; it points to the sky, echoing Li Daoyuan's Chang'an across the centuries. The Xi'an City Wall surrounding the city was built in the Ming dynasty, but its foundations are precisely the Sui-Tang Chang'an imperial city that Li Daoyuan recorded. In the Commentary on the Water Classic, he wrote: "Chang'an City was the old capital of the Han; the Sui built Daxing City."—a few words spanning a thousand years. Standing on the wall today and looking out, the Wei is like a silken ribbon, the Zhongnan Mountains like a screen—Li Daoyuan once gazed at this same river, recording its past and present life on bamboo slips, stroke by stroke.

stops.title: Stop Five: The Luo River—A Thousand Years of Buddha Light at the Divine Capital Luoyang
stops.content: The Luo River is not long, but it holds an exalted place in the Commentary on the Water Classic. Li Daoyuan took the Northern Wei capital Luoyang as the central coordinate of his commentary—he himself served as an official in Luoyang, and the Luo was the river he knew best. "The Luo River originates in Shangluo County of the capital region," flowing northward, passing through Luoyang. Li Daoyuan's account of the palaces, temples, bridges, and gardens on both banks of the Luo forms a panoramic picture of Northern Wei Luoyang. The White Horse Temple on the banks of the Luo was the first officially established Buddhist monastery after Buddhism's introduction to China. In the Commentary on the Water Classic, Li Daoyuan recorded in detail the temple's origin: Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han dreamed of a golden man, sent envoys westward to seek the Dharma, and a white horse carried the sutras back—"a white horse carrying sutras" became one of the most moving images in Chinese cultural history. The temple's Cool Terrace and Cloud-Equal Pagoda were all noted by Li Daoyuan. Today, the White Horse Temple still thrives with incense, its bells crossing two millennia to ring on the banks of the Luo. On the south bank of the Luo, the Longmen Grottoes were in their early stages in Li Daoyuan's time. In his commentary, he recorded the "stone niches" on both banks of the Yi River—the term used for Buddhist caves at that time. After Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei moved the capital to Luoyang, the imperial court began large-scale carving of the Longmen Grottoes, creating today's world-renowned treasure house of stone carving art. And as the Luo River continues eastward, at the Shaolin Temple at the foot of Shaoshi Mountain in Dengfeng, the bells and chimes of the Chan Buddhist ancestral temple harmonize with the Luo River's murmuring. Li Daoyuan, with the Luo River as his thread, strung together not only geography but also the complete cultural arc of Buddhism—from its introduction at White Horse Temple, to its glorious apex at Longmen, to its union of Chan and martial arts at Shaolin Temple. Li Daoyuan's commentary on the Luo River has the strongest "sense of presence"—for he lived in Luoyang. He crossed the Luo River's pontoon bridge every day—"on the Luo River there was formerly a floating bridge, with boats as piers"—walking on the swaying planks, listening to the river murmuring beneath. On the banks of the Luo, he saw women washing clothes, old men fishing, merchants ferrying across—"ceaseless from dawn till dusk." Li Daoyuan in his commentary particularly recorded the legend of the Luo River goddess Fufei, citing Cao Zhi's "Rhapsody on the Luo River Goddess": "Her form was like a startled swan, graceful as a swimming dragon"—a passage of immortal prose suddenly drifting into a geographical commentary: this is the unique charm of the Commentary on the Water Classic. Li Daoyuan eventually met a violent death—while serving as Regional Inspector of Guanyou, he was murdered by a rebel general, only fifty-nine years old. He died before completing the Commentary on the Water Classic; this forty-volume magnum opus was meant to go even further. But the words he left behind were enough: 1,252 rivers, over 4,000 place names, 437 cited texts, 302 steles recorded—behind these numbers stands a Northern Wei scholar who built a monument to the mountains and rivers of Huaxia with his steps and his ink. As he himself said in his preface: "The greatest of all things under heaven is water—it floats the sky and bears the earth"—water moistens all things, and the Commentary on the Water Classic moistens a thousand ages.

stops.title: Stop Six: The Han River—The Cultural Confluence Where Rivers Pay Homage
stops.content: The Han River is the Yangtze's largest tributary, originating deep in the Qinling Mountains from Mount Bozhong, flowing southeast through the Hanzhong Basin and the Jianghan Plain, joining the Yangtze at Wuhan. The Commentary on the Water Classic names it the "Mian River" and devotes three full volumes to this golden waterway linking Qinlong with Jing-Chu. Li Daoyuan wrote: "The Han River emerges from Mount Bozhong in Didao County, Longxi." He traced the Han's source deep into the Qinling Mountains and meticulously recorded the plank roads and passes along the upper reaches. The most moving stretch of the Han River is at Xiangyang. Li Daoyuan recorded Xiangyang City as "bounded by the Han River to the north and Xian Mountain to the south," occupying a strategically vital position. Here the Han makes a wide bend, forming a natural harbor. The remarkably well-preserved Xiangyang City Wall, whose Linhan Gate directly faces the surging Han, has been the throat of north-south transportation since its founding in the Han dynasty. During the Three Kingdoms period, Zhuge Liang lived in seclusion at Longzhong west of Xiangyang by the Han River—"I was a commoner, plowing fields in Nanyang." Liu Bei's three visits to Zhuge Liang's thatched cottage took place on this very riverside. In the Commentary on the Water Classic, Li Daoyuan recorded Longzhong's location: "The Mian River flows eastward, passing Longzhong." Although he could not visit in person, he cited local accounts to describe the precise location of Zhuge Liang's former residence. The Han River is also a cultural link between north and south. Li Bai wrote, "The Han River's waves stretch far, the clouds and rain fly over Mount Wu." Du Fu sighed, "The Han River, too, should flow northwestward." The Han River of Li Daoyuan's writing bore not only the merchant boats plying north and south, but also the continuous flow of Huaxia civilization from the Qin-Han through the Northern and Southern Dynasties. Today, standing on the Xiangyang City Wall, watching the Han roll on, a thousand sails racing—this great river, whose every ferry and every bridge was meticulously recorded in the Commentary on the Water Classic, still surges on, night and day, without pause. If Li Daoyuan could travel here again, he would surely add to his commentary: "The Han River is as before, but the city walls have been renewed."
